passages.t: ‘With all of us who are alive here today’
passages.happening:
The second and longest address of Moses begins. He gathers the whole people. “Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully” (verse 1).

Then he says something startling. “The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today” (verses 2-3).

God spoke with them ‘face to face out of the fire on the mountain’ (verse 4). Moses stood between God and the people to pass on his word, ‘because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A covenant is a binding relationship, sealed by an oath, with duties on both sides. In Deuteronomy the word names the whole bond between the LORD and Israel. The Ten Commandments are its core terms.

Verse 3 is not true as plain history, and Moses knows it. The covenant at Horeb was made forty years earlier, with the parents of the people in front of him. Most of these hearers were children then, or not yet born. Moses says it was made not with their fathers but with them, and he says it to make a point. The covenant is not something that happened to other people long ago. Whoever hears it is the one it is made with.

This is how the whole book speaks. Its favorite word is ‘today’. Each generation that reads Deuteronomy is placed at the foot of the mountain and addressed as though it were there.

‘Face to face’ does not mean that Israel saw a face. Chapter 4 insisted that they saw no form at all. It means that God spoke to them directly, with no one in between. Verse 5 then adds that the people were afraid, and that Moses stood between. Both are true. God addressed them all, and they needed a go-between. The end of the chapter tells how that came about.

Many scholars compare the shape of this covenant with treaties of the ancient world, in which a great king named himself, told what he had done for his subjects, and then laid down the terms of loyalty. Chapter 5 reads like the heart of such a document. The book introduction says more about this.
passages.later:
Exodus tells of the first making of this covenant, when the people answered together, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exodus 24:7).

The prophet Jeremiah promised that God would one day make the covenant new, in the heart: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

The letter to the Hebrews sets the fire and darkness of this mountain beside what Christians have come to: ‘to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant’ (Hebrews 12:24).
passages.asks: Moses will not let his hearers treat God's covenant as their parents' affair. Ask whether your faith is something you have received for yourself, or something that belongs to the people who raised you. And hear the word ‘today’. Ask what God is saying to you now, and not only what he said to others once.

passages.t: The first words: God alone, his name, his day
passages.happening:
Now God speaks, and Moses quotes him. Before any command comes a statement: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (verse 6).

Then the commands. “You shall have no other gods before Me” (verse 7). No idol is to be made, in the form of anything in the sky, on the earth or in the water (verse 8). Israel must not bow down to such things, ‘for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God’ (verse 9).

“You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain” (verse 11).

“Observe the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (verse 12). Six days are for work. On the seventh no one works: not son or daughter, not servant, not ox or donkey, not the foreigner in the town, ‘so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do’ (verse 14). “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
These are the Ten Commandments, called in Hebrew the ten words. They were first given in Exodus 20. Moses repeats them here almost word for word.

Everything depends on verse 6. God does not begin with a demand. He begins with what he has done. Israel was in slavery, and he brought them out. The commands that follow are addressed to people already rescued. They describe life in freedom.

The Bible never numbers the ten, and Jews and Christians have counted them in different ways. Jewish tradition counts verse 6 as the first word. Catholic and Lutheran churches join the commands about other gods and about images into one and divide the last command in two. Most Orthodox and Reformed churches count other gods and images as two. The words are the same in every case.

‘No other gods’ was a hard demand in a world where every nation had many. The command against idols follows from chapter 4: Israel saw no form, so no form may stand for God. ‘Jealous’ is the jealousy of a husband who will not share his wife's love with a rival. That is why the prophets later picture idol worship as adultery.

The command about God's name concerns more than careless speech. The Hebrew speaks of lifting up the name for emptiness: using God's name to back a false oath, to curse, or to bend him to one's own will.

The Sabbath command shows how Moses preaches. In Exodus the reason for the day is creation: God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Here the reason is the rescue from Egypt. In the ancient world rest belonged to the powerful, who took it at the cost of those under them. The Sabbath broke that order once a week. The command reaches past the head of the house to his children, his servants, his animals and the foreigner without land. People who had been slaves were forbidden to become masters who never let anyone stop.

Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies now. Some keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, some keep the seventh day, and some hold that the day was a shadow fulfilled in Christ and leave it to conscience.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the other reason for the Sabbath: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11).

Jesus said what the day was for: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Paul wrote to a church troubled about holy days: “Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath” (Colossians 2:16).
passages.hard:
Verse 9 speaks of God ‘visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations’. Does God punish children for what their parents did?

Read by itself the line sounds like guilt handed down. But this same book forbids it in court: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (24:16). The prophet Ezekiel says the same of God's own judgment: “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20).

Readers hold these together in several ways.

Many Jewish and Christian readers stress the closing words, ‘of those who hate Me’. On this reading the verse speaks of children who carry on their parents' rebellion.

Others note that three or four generations is the size of a household living under one roof in ancient Israel. On this reading the verse describes how a family's idol worship harms everyone in the house within one lifetime.

Others point to the contrast with verse 10. Judgment reaches three or four generations. God's loving devotion reaches ‘a thousand generations’.

On any of these readings the verse is a warning about how far sin spreads, set beside a promise that mercy spreads much further. It does not say that you are being punished for what your father or mother did.
passages.asks: God names himself as the one who brings people out of slavery before he asks anything of them. Ask whether you hear his commands as the words of a rescuer or of a taskmaster. And think about the Sabbath. Ask who rests when you rest, and whether anyone works without stopping so that you can live as you do.

passages.t: The neighbor: parents, life, marriage, property, truth, desire
passages.happening:
The commands turn to other people. “Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God has commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land” (verse 16).

Then four short ones. “You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (verses 17-20).

The last goes inside. ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or field’, or his servants, his animals, ‘or anything that belongs to your neighbor’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The word ‘honor’ comes from the Hebrew word for heavy: to give someone weight. For adults it meant caring for parents and respecting them in their old age, not only obeying them as a child. Paul calls it ‘the first commandment with a promise’ (Ephesians 6:2).

The next three are two Hebrew words each. They guard a neighbor's life, a neighbor's marriage and a neighbor's goods. In Deuteronomy the last five commands are joined together by the word ‘and’, so that they read as one piece.

False witness belonged first at the town gate, where cases were heard. A false witness could cost a man his life or his land.

The last command is different from the rest. The Hebrew verb means to desire what belongs to someone else. Some interpreters think it includes the scheming that leads to taking. Others hold that it names the inward desire itself. Either way it reaches beneath anything a judge can see. The law collections of other ancient nations dealt with acts that a court could prove. No court can convict a desire. Israel's covenant ends by naming one.

There is a small difference from Exodus here. In Exodus the neighbor's house comes first and his wife is listed within it. In Deuteronomy the wife is given a sentence to herself, and a field is added. Some see a higher view of the wife in this. Others see the concerns of a people about to own farmland.
passages.later:
Jesus quoted these commands as God's will, and pressed them inward as the last command does: “But I tell you that anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment” (Matthew 5:22).

Paul says they are held together by one thing. The commandments ‘are summed up in this one decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself”’ (Romans 13:9).

He also says it was this last command that showed him his own heart: ‘I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, “Do not covet”’ (Romans 7:7).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Honor your father and your mother’ mean that a person must obey or stay with a parent who does harm?

No. The note on Exodus 20, where this command is first given, says what must be said here too.

These words must never be used against a child who is being harmed. No one may use ‘obey your parents’ to keep a child quiet about abuse, or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.

For grown children, honoring a parent can mean care and respect in their old age, as Jesus said. It never means pretending that harm was not harm, or going back into danger. Honor and safety are not enemies.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The commands move from acts that can be seen to a desire that cannot. Ask which of them you keep on the outside while breaking it within. And think about the neighbor these commands protect. Ask whose name, marriage or goods are safer because you are near, and whose are not.

passages.t: ‘Go near and listen’: the people ask for a go-between
passages.happening:
Moses tells what happened after God spoke. God wrote the commands on two tablets of stone, ‘He added nothing more’ (verse 22).

The leaders came to Moses in fear. They had heard God's voice and lived. But they said, ‘this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer’ (verse 25). They asked Moses to go near in their place: ‘Then you can tell us everything the LORD our God tells you; we will listen and obey’ (verse 27).

God heard, and approved. “They have done well in all that they have spoken. If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever” (verses 28-29).

So the people went back to their tents, and Moses stayed with God to receive the rest of the law (verses 30-31). Moses ends: ‘you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
This scene explains why the rest of Deuteronomy exists. The ten words were spoken by God to everyone. Everything after them came through Moses, because the people asked for it to be so. The laws of chapters 6 to 26 are what Moses received while the people waited in their tents.

The people's fear is not mocked. God says they have spoken well. To stand before the living God is not a small thing, and they are right to know it.

Then comes one of the most tender sentences in the book. ‘If only they had such a heart.’ God does not doubt that they mean their promise. He knows it will not last. The trouble is not in the law. It is in the heart, and a heart cannot be changed by a command.

Deuteronomy returns to this again and again. In chapter 10 Israel is told to circumcise its heart. In chapter 30 God promises to do it himself. The longing of verse 29 is answered there.

The last picture is a straight road. Israel is to walk in God's ways without turning aside to the right or the left. The book uses the picture often.
passages.later:
Later in this book Moses looks back to this very request and says God will answer it again: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

Exodus tells the same scene: “Speak to us yourself and we will listen,” they said to Moses. “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die” (Exodus 20:19).

The prophet Ezekiel carried God's answer to the longing of verse 29: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The New Testament says that the go-between the people asked for has been given in full: “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).
passages.asks: God looked at a sincere promise and wished for a heart that could keep it. Ask what you have promised God in a strong moment and not kept. Then ask him for what he wished for in verse 29. A changed heart is something he gives.
